aAbout: GodsView AI is a hosted live world map: a 2D map (MapLibre GL and deck.gl) with a Cesium 3D globe, fed by OpenSky aircraft, aisstream.io ships, satellites, earthquakes, NASA fire data, weather and news. Its signature piece is the Ops Center, which merges duplicate reports of the same event from agencies like USGS, GDACS and GDELT and scores every incident from 0 to 100, with country risk ratings. A free account opens the map; Pro unlocks the full camera catalogue, the photoreal globe, alerts and flight replay.
aStrengths: GodsView AI is the operational tool: the Ops Center turns a firehose of agency reports into a scored, deduplicated incident register with country risk — something neither God's Eye View nor most live maps attempt. Add Pro alerts (emergency squawks, quakes, watch areas), flight replay, a news video wall, briefs you can export, and a lifetime pricing option, and it's the better pick for journalists and researchers who monitor the world daily from any browser.
bAbout: God's Eye View is an open-source 3D world globe simulator — 'a spy-satellite simulator in your browser, except the data is real.' It renders Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles through Cesium and layers live aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic and public cameras from open sources, all processed locally in your browser. It went viral in 2026 (#1 on GitHub Trending, 61,000+ stars) for its voice-controlled AI agent, cockpit view and sensor-style visual modes. It is software you run yourself — via Pinokio one-click, a terminal install, or Docker — not a website you open.

bLink.label: WorldEye: the God's Eye View alternative

bStrengths: God's Eye View is the more spectacular and the more ownable tool: a photorealistic 3D globe with cockpit view, 3D aircraft models, sensor looks (FLIR, night vision) and a scene director for cinematic tours — all free, all running on your machine with data you can inspect, extend and keep. Its voice agent genuinely has no equivalent here: you talk to the globe and it flies, tracks and annotates. For creators, tinkerers and anyone who wants the globe itself to be the experience, nothing hosted matches it.
betterAnswer: They're not rivals so much as answers to different questions — and they're definitely not the same product. God's Eye View is free software: the most cinematic live globe ever open-sourced, voice-controlled, running on your machine, with no alerts or incident desk. GodsView AI is a hosted service: less cinematic, but with a scored Ops Center, alerts and replay behind a reasonably priced Pro tier. People who want to *watch* the world install God's Eye View; people who want to be *notified about* it open GodsView AI.

faqs.a: No. GodsView AI states on its own site that it is a separate, unaffiliated hosted product. God's Eye View is an open-source project by Bilawal Sidhu that you install and run yourself; GodsView AI is a hosted map at godsviewai.com built by a different maker.
faqs.q: Is GodsView AI the same as God's Eye View?

faqs.a: Both, differently. God's Eye View is free software with no paid tier at all (optional third-party keys can meter — the voice agent uses your own OpenAI credit). GodsView AI is freemium: a free account tier with ads and limits, and Pro at $10.99/month, $99.99/year or $199.99 lifetime.

GodsView AI claims a catalogue of about 229,000 public cameras, but only 2 open on its free tier — the rest need Pro. God's Eye View's CCTV Mesh layer states a cap of about 4,000 cameras, all available once you're running it. WorldEye's directory lists 74,229, open on the free map.
God's Eye View needs no account — you run it locally. GodsView AI requires a free account before the map opens. (WorldEye's free globe, for contrast, needs neither install nor account.)
faqs.q: Do either of them work without an account?

faqs.a: GodsView AI. Its Ops Center merges reports from USGS, GDACS, NASA EONET, NWS, WHO, IODA and GDELT, scores incidents 0–100 and ranks country risk, and Pro adds alerts. God's Eye View shows live layers beautifully but has no news or incident desk.
faqs.q: Which is better for following breaking news?

faqs.a: Not as an app — it runs on your own computer (Windows, macOS or Linux) in a WebGL browser. GodsView AI runs in any modern browser, including mobile browsers.

intro: First, the confusion: GodsView AI and God's Eye View are different, unaffiliated products — GodsView AI says so on its own site. God's Eye View is the viral open-source project by Bilawal Sidhu: a photorealistic 3D globe you install and run on your own computer, free forever. GodsView AI is a hosted live map at godsviewai.com — flights, ships, satellites, incidents and cameras in the browser, free with an account, with a Pro tier and an incident-scoring Ops Center. This page compares them properly, because search results keep mixing them up.
pricingA: GodsView AI is free with a free account — with banner ads, a 30-minute live-viewing pause (reload to continue), one AI question a day and two open cameras. Pro costs $10.99/month, $99.99/year or $199.99 as a one-time lifetime plan (no free trial), and unlocks the full ~229,000-camera catalogue, the photoreal 3D globe, military aircraft, NOTAMs, alerts and flight replay.
pricingB: There is no God's Eye View price or subscription — the software is free and open source. The README's own cost table is honest about the edges: most layers cost $0 with no signup; a free-key tier (AISStream, NASA FIRMS, Cesium ion within quota) unlocks more; the voice agent spends your own OpenAI credit with a $2 warning and $5 hard cap per session; and photoreal tiles through a direct Google key are metered by Google.

verdictA: Choose GodsView AI if you want a hosted monitoring desk — scored incidents, alerts, replay — that opens in any browser and asks nothing of your computer.
verdictB: Choose God's Eye View if you want the immersive photoreal globe, voice control and total ownership of the tool — and you're happy installing it yourself.
verdictLine: God's Eye View is the famous one — free software you run yourself, all spectacle and voice control. GodsView AI is the hosted service — less cinematic, but it scores incidents, sends alerts and replays flights. Same genre, opposite delivery.
worldEye: WorldEye sits between these two in a specific way: like GodsView AI it's a hosted globe that opens in the browser — but unlike GodsView AI it needs no account at all for the free map. Like God's Eye View it leads with a real 3D globe — but you never install anything. Its 74,229 public cameras across 105 countries sit between the two camera claims, its layers (flights, ships, satellites, weather, quakes, fires) are free, and Pro ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) adds an OSINT toolkit and intel feeds rather than an incident register.
